clue.text: Villain gesturing angrily unlikely to be this

definitions.text: Villain gesturing angrily unlikely to be this

indicators.note: gesturing angrily suggests wild flailing, so the letters of the two words before it are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A wicked character waving his arms in fury is hardly the type to make a public show of his goodness.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the sixteen letters of VILLAIN GESTURING rearrange into the phrase, and a villain is the last person to parade moral virtue.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostentatious displays of right-thinking opinions are what a villain would hardly bother making, so the whole clue paints the term.

clue.text: Smoke (sort of) seen rising in the pavilion

indicators.note: rising says the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone spots a wisp of smoke climbing inside the cricket pavilion.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'seen' into the definition; it is a link word, and 'in' is the signal that the letters are concealed. In a down clue 'rising' reads them bottom to top, so EPAV in 'thE PAVilion' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: Inhaling from an e-cigarette is a modern kind of smoking, hence the hedge in brackets.

clue.text: Complaining one side's weak

parts.note: right is one side, abbreviated R
ailing means sickly or weak

explanation.surface: Someone moans that one flank of the team is feeble.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail against something is to protest bitterly about it, so the participle means grumbling.

clue.text: Pulled a muscle touring North America

indicators.note: touring means travelling round, so the scrambled letters go round the abbreviation
a pulled muscle is strained out of shape, so the letters of the words after it are pulled into a new order

explanation.surface: An athlete strains a muscle while on a tour of the USA.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulled' rearranges A MUSCLE to UCLESAM, and 'touring' puts it round N to give UNCLESAM.
explanation.definitionFit: The bearded figure in a top hat is the long-standing personification of the United States.

clue.text: Over 50 the end of the line? They're having you on!

indicators.note: over says one piece covers the other, so the railway stops are put round the numeral

parts.note: buffers stand at the end of a railway line
L is the Roman numeral for 50

explanation.surface: A railway buff at the end of the line, aged over fifty, is mocked as a joker.
explanation.walkthrough: BUFFERS are the barriers at the end of a railway track; putting them over L (50) gives B-L-UFFERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who pretend or deceive are people pulling your leg, the idiom of having someone on.

clue.text: Fat doll? Heavens, that's unusual!

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters of the two words are set in another arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at a strangely plump toy figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' rearranges DOLL and HEAVENS; 'that's' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a jokey name for the rolls of flab around the waist, so it stands for body fat.

clue.text: Friend of Trump supposedly following a trend

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
a rage is a craze or trend, as in 'all the rage'

explanation.surface: A political ally of Trump is said to be merely chasing the latest fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supposedly' belongs to the definition, hedging the friendship. Nigel Farage is a British politician who led UKIP and the Brexit Party.
explanation.definitionFit: The British politician has been a prominent supporter and associate of Donald Trump, at least by reputation.

clue.text: Not concise from the outset — War and Peace, perhaps, a good example

indicators.note: not says the letter that follows is excluded from the big book

parts.note: Tolstoy's novel is a huge epic tome, an example of a very long book

indicators.note: from the outset picks the opening letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A reviewer says Tolstoy's novel is anything but brief, yet a fine illustration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' takes away the first letter of 'concise' (C) from EPIC TOME. 'Perhaps' marks the novel as an example of the type.
explanation.definitionFit: A perfect specimen or embodiment of a quality is its quintessence, the classic instance of it.

clue.text: Croatian goals causing shock outcome?

definitions.note: a shock of hair; the question mark flags the play on shock

parts.note: Split is a city on the coast of Croatia
ends are aims or goals

explanation.surface: A sports report on a Croatian side's goals that produced a surprise result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shock' reads as a surprise, but here it is a mass of hair, and frayed tips are one thing that happens to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Frayed tips are a result found on a shock, meaning a thick mop of hair, hence the playful question mark.

clue.text: What it costs to keep new royal

indicators.note: to keep means to hold inside, so the cost goes round the letter

parts.note: the price is what something costs

explanation.surface: Someone asks how much it costs to maintain a newly born royal.
explanation.definitionFit: A son of a monarch is a member of the royal family, so the noun sense of royal fits.

clue.text: Finished with a thousand — unfortunate it's too much

parts.note: over means ended or finished
K stands for a thousand
ill can mean unlucky, as in ill fortune

explanation.surface: Finishing on a thousand runs is sadly excessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Excess beyond what is needed is the idiom for something done to a needless, excessive degree.

clue.text: Become dispirited and stop working

definitions.meaning: to lose heart, or literally to lose one's spirit
to break down, as a machine that packs in

explanation.surface: Someone loses heart and quits the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dispirited' is a pun: the phrase literally means to release the spirit, and it is also said of a machine that conks out.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means both to give up hope and, of a machine, to cease functioning.

clue.text: Use influence to withdraw fleeces worn by king

parts.note: to pull out is to withdraw

indicators.note: worn by means the clothing piece goes on the wearer, so the letter sits inside the swindles

parts.note: fleeces as a verb means cheats, as stings do
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A monarch is draped in woollen fleeces, and someone pulls them off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleeces' looks like clothing worn by a king, but it is the verb: STINGS, meaning swindles, with R inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Like a puppeteer working a marionette, this idiom means to exert hidden influence behind the scenes.

clue.text: See 1
Ready to turn round when attack begins

parts.note: set means ready, as in ready, steady, go

indicators.note: to turn round signals the short word that follows is read backwards

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
a bout is an attack or fit, as of illness

explanation.surface: Something primed to wheel round the moment an assault starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attack' wants to be the definition, but it is BOUT, and 'begins' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To start on a task with determination is a phrasal verb for starting it.

clue.text: Rubberneckers going round city

indicators.note: the long word goes round, or encloses, the city's letters

explanation.surface: Gawping onlookers are touring a city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swiss capital is a city, so it is a straightforward example.

clue.text: Caught Courtois finally taking a breather in goal

indicators.note: in says the pieces before it sit inside the target

parts.note: an end is a goal or aim

indicators.note: finally picks the closing letter of the goalkeeper's name

parts.note: a nare is a nostril, through which one breathes

explanation.surface: The Belgian goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois finally pauses for breath in his goalmouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breather' looks like a rest, but it is a nostril; the nostril and the last letter of Courtois both go inside the goal word.
explanation.definitionFit: Trapped, as in a snare, is the sense of being captured.

clue.text: Young British journalist attached to Times

parts.note: by means multiplied by, as in three by four

explanation.surface: A young British reporter has joined the staff of The Times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Young' reads as youthful, but it is a surname: Toby Young is a British journalist. 'Attached' just joins TO to BY.
explanation.definitionFit: The journalist Toby Young, a British writer and commentator, is named by his surname in the clue.

clue.text: Habitually complain about second-class seat

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the nagging phrase goes round the grade letter

parts.note: to be a nag is to complain habitually
B is the second grade, after A

explanation.surface: Someone forever grumbles about their inferior chair.
explanation.walkthrough: BE A NAG goes round B, giving BEAN-B-AG.
explanation.definitionFit: A large fabric sack of beads you sit on is a kind of soft chair or seat.

clue.text: Walks near sea and sand — please get dressed!

indicators.note: to get dressed is to be put in order, as troops dress their ranks, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: At the beach, someone begs the sunbathers to put some clothes on.
explanation.definitionFit: Seaside promenades are paved walkways along the shore.

clue.text: Sack young lady after insult

indicators.note: after puts the word for a girl behind the slang for an insult

parts.note: dis is slang for insult or disrespect
a miss is a young unmarried woman

explanation.surface: Someone fires a girl after she was rude.
explanation.definitionFit: To fire someone from a job is to let them go, the verb sense of sack.

clue.text: Move top one, right?

parts.note: best means top or finest
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to shift the leading one to the right.
explanation.definitionFit: To rouse oneself into action is the old verb meaning to get going.

clue.text: Sculpted arse with enthusiasm but lack of skill

indicators.note: sculpted means shaped and remodelled, so the letters are reshaped into a new order

explanation.surface: A keen but clumsy sculptor carves a bottom with gusto.
explanation.definitionFit: Clumsy work lacking professional competence shows ineptitude, the quality of a dabbler.

clue.text: Don't hang around! It's a step up

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the step is read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: pas is a dance step, from French

explanation.surface: Someone urges haste, saying it is only a short climb.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for as soon as possible, it is an urging to hurry, like the exclamation.

clue.text: Men taking the bait and ringing

parts.note: OR, other ranks, are soldiers who are not officers
a fish that is biting is taking the bait

explanation.surface: Anglers hooking fish and telephoning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringing' looks like a telephone sound, but it means encircling.
explanation.definitionFit: Circling round something, as a planet round a star, is going round it in a ring.

clue.text: Qualities beginning to hold one back

indicators.note: back says the whole combination is read backwards
to hold means to contain, so the start goes round the numeral

parts.note: the start is the beginning
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Character qualities begin by restraining a person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To hold' puts I inside START, making STIART, and 'back' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: Distinguishing characteristics of a person are their features or attributes.

clue.text: Fiercely determined Spice Girl takes part in this (off-key)

indicators.note: takes part in means joins in, so the singer goes inside the rearranged word
off-key means out of tune, so the letters of the little word are thrown out of order

parts.note: Geri Halliwell was Ginger Spice in the Spice Girls pop group

explanation.surface: A pop star sings out of tune while performing a song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off-key' rearranges the little word to TISH, and 'takes part in' puts the singer inside it. The Spice Girls were a 1990s British girl band.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiercely determined suggests a big cat's ferocity, being like a big striped cat.

clue.text: Notice May's supporters keeping close to Boris does make sense

parts.note: an ad, short for advertisement, is a notice

indicators.note: keeping means holding inside, so the party goes round the letter

parts.note: the Democratic Unionist Party propped up Theresa May's minority government

indicators.note: close to picks the last letter of the name

explanation.surface: A political advert on Theresa May's allies who are staying near Boris Johnson.
explanation.walkthrough: The DUP, a Northern Irish party, backed Theresa May's government in 2017-19; S, the last letter of Boris, goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Being logical or consistent is the idiom used of an argument that holds together.
